latin.509: PLAC. More eorum qui submerguntur, obvium quodque arripit vir doctus: sed frustra. Significet enim phrasis εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν apud Graecos incipere litem, num sequitur, idem verbum cum quovis alio nomine constructum pro incipere usurpari? Num ex. g. εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον, vel εἰς τὴν πόλιν, erit incipere domum vel urbem, aut ita incipere esse in domo vel urbe, ut antea non fueris?
latin.510: Perperam laudatur locus Act. 1. 21. nam ingredi & egredi Hebraismus est, neque nativitatem neque mortem significans, sed conversationem, & vel publicorum vel privatorum officiorum functiones. vide Bez. Ann. in illum locum.
latin.511: Alter quoque Heb. 1. 6. virum doctum refellit: intelligendus enim non est de nativitate Christi, sed de secundo eius gloriosissimo adventu, ut patet ex verbis Apostoli, & toto Ps. 97. unde sunt desumpta. Caeterum hanc viri docti responsionem refutavit Bellarminus multis rationibus lib. 4. de amiss. Grat. cap. 3. & post eum Chamierus, sed brevius, lib. 1. de hom. corrupt. cap. 5. §. 9.
latin.512: Quidni ergo dixerim peccata nostra in Christum εἰσελθεῖν, cum Scriptura dicat, ea venisse in Christum? Dominus fecit venire, vel incurrere in eum iniquitates omnium nostrum. Esai. LIII. 6. Et similiter, peccatum Adae in nos ἐλθεῖν, in nos venisse, quia eius reatum sustinemus, id est, quia illud imputatum nobis est? Itaque quanquam introire simpliciter positum, non sit idem quod imputare, tamen peccatum introire, vel venire in aliquem, si res aut locus, ubi phrasis habetur, ita exigit, potest idem esse quod peccatum illud ipsi imputari.
latin.513: PLAC. Non potuit diligentius Pighii expositio defendi, quam sit a viro docto hoc quidem in loco: nullum enim lapidem non movet ut extorqueat e manibus orthodoxorum argumentum, quod soliti sunt adversus Pelagium & Pighium ex verbis Apostoli ducere, per unum hominem peccatum introiit in mundum. Sed frustra laborat. Expugnari veritas non potest. Quid est, quare sibi dari Vir doctus postulet, compositum εἰσελθεῖν, nihil significatione differre a simplici ἐλθεῖν? Aut quis ferat dicentem peccata nostra introiisse in Christum, aut per nos peccatum intrasse in Christum? Nonne talem locutionem pia refugit conscientia?
latin.514: Locus Esai. LIII. 6. ad rem non est, tum quia non est idem verbum: הִפְגִּיעַ enim non est fecit ingredi seu introire, sed fecit occurrere, vel incurrere; tum quia iniquitas eo loco non ipsum peccatum, sed poenam peccati significat. Occurrit enim Christo, incurrit, irruit in eum, &, si ita vis, intravit in eum non peccatum, sed sola peccati poena. Hic autem peccatum a peccati poena distinguitur: sequitur enim, & per peccatum mors. Itaque probari non potest idem esse posse, peccatum in aliquem ingredi, & peccatum alicui imputari. Quod si peccatum, quatenus a poena distinguitur, ingressum est in Christum, quid est cur Christus non potuerit dici peccator? Si hoc est absurdum, illud quoque absurdum esse confitendum est.

pass_a.509: PLAC: Like drowning men the learned man seizes whatever floats—but in vain. Grant that among the Greeks εἰς τὸ δικαστήριον εἰσελθεῖν means to begin a suit: does the same verb with any other noun mean 'begin'? Will εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὸν οἶκον or εἰς τὴν πόλιν mean to begin a house or city, or to begin being in house or city as if you were not there before?
pass_a.510: Acts 1:21 is wrongly praised: going in and out is a Hebraism for conversation and the discharge of public or private offices—not birth or death. See Beza's Annot. on the place.
pass_a.511: Heb 1:6 also refutes him: it is not Christ's nativity but his second most glorious coming, as the Apostle's words and all of Ps 97 (from which they are taken) show. Bellarmine answered this learned reply with many reasons (De amiss. grat. 4.3), and after him Chamier more briefly (De hom. corrupt. 1.5.9).
pass_a.512: GAR: Why then may I not say our sins εἰσελθεῖν into Christ, when Scripture says they came upon him? The Lord made the iniquities of us all to come or fall upon him (Isa 53:6). Likewise Adam's sin ἐλθεῖν upon us—came upon us—because we bear its reatus, that is, because it is imputed to us. So though 'enter' alone is not 'impute,' yet if the matter and place of the phrase require it, sin's entering or coming upon someone can be the same as its being imputed to him.
pass_a.513: PLAC: Pighius's reading could not be defended more carefully than the learned man does here—he leaves no stone unmoved to wrest from the orthodox the argument they draw against Pelagius and Pighius from 'through one man sin entered into the world.' He labors in vain; truth cannot be stormed. Why demand that compound εἰσελθεῖν differ in sense not at all from simple ἐλθεῖν? Or who can bear hearing that our sins entered into Christ, or that through us sin entered into him? Does not a pious conscience flee such speech?
pass_a.514: Isa 53:6 is off the point: first the verb is not the same—הִפְגִּיעַ is not 'made to enter' but 'made to meet/fall upon'; second, iniquity there means the penalty of sin, not the sin itself. What met, fell on, rushed into him—if you will, entered him—was not sin but only sin's penalty. Here sin is distinguished from its penalty: 'and through sin, death' follows. So it cannot be proved that sin's entering someone and sin's being imputed to him are the same. If sin as distinct from penalty entered Christ, why could he not be called a sinner? If that is absurd, so is the other. Tip before the imputatum-est substitution reductio.

509: PLAC. After the manner of those who are drowning, the learned man seizes whatever meets him: but in vain. For grant that the phrase eis to dikasterion eiselthein among the Greeks signifies to begin a suit, does it follow that the same verb constructed with any other noun is used for 'to begin'? Will, for example, eiselthein eis ton oikon, or eis ten polin, be to begin a house or a city, or so to begin to be in a house or city, that you were not there before?
510: The place Acts 1. 21. is wrongly praised: for to go in and to go out is a Hebraism, signifying neither birth nor death, but conversation, and the functions of either public or private offices. See Beza's Annot. on that place.
511: The other place also, Heb. 1. 6., refutes the learned man: for it is not to be understood of Christ's nativity, but of his second most glorious advent, as is plain from the Apostle's words, and from the whole of Ps. 97. from which they are taken. Moreover Bellarmine refuted this reply of the learned man with many reasons in book 4. de amiss. Grat. chapter 3. and after him Chamier, but more briefly, in book 1. de hom. corrupt. chapter 5. section 9.
512: Why then may I not say that our sins eiselthein into Christ, when Scripture says they came into Christ? The Lord made the iniquities of us all to come, or to fall upon him. Isaiah 53. 6. And likewise, that Adam's sin elthein upon us, came upon us, because we sustain its reatus, that is, because it has been imputed to us? And so although to enter simply put is not the same as to impute, yet for sin to enter, or to come upon someone, if the matter or place where the phrase is held so requires, can be the same as for that sin to be imputed to him.
513: PLAC. Pighius's exposition could not have been defended more carefully than it is by the learned man in this place: for he moves no stone that he may wrest from the orthodox the argument which they are accustomed to draw against Pelagius and Pighius from the Apostle's words, through one man sin entered into the world. But he labors in vain. Truth cannot be stormed. What is it, why the learned man demands to be granted to himself, that the compound eiselthein differs in signification not at all from the simple elthein? Or who will bear one saying that our sins entered into Christ, or that through us sin entered into Christ? Does not a pious conscience flee such a locution?
514: The place Isaiah 53. 6. is not to the point, both because it is not the same verb: for hiphgia is not 'he made to enter' or 'to go in,' but 'he made to meet,' or 'to fall upon'; and because iniquity in that place signifies not the sin itself, but the penalty of sin. For it met Christ, falls upon him, rushes upon him, and, if you will, entered into him—not sin, but only the penalty of sin. But here sin is distinguished from the penalty of sin: for there follows, and through sin death. And so it cannot be proved that it can be the same, for sin to enter into someone, and for sin to be imputed to someone. But if sin, insofar as it is distinguished from penalty, entered into Christ, what is there why Christ could not have been called a sinner? If this is absurd, that also must be confessed to be absurd.
